lines.text: That close door button? It probably does nothing.
lines.see: Tight on the lift's close-door button glowing amber as it is pressed, slow push

lines.text: You press it. Again. And again. The doors don't move any faster.
lines.see: Pull back inside the lift: the button flashes on every press, the doors stay wide open

lines.text: So here's what's actually behind the panel.
lines.see: Camera dives into the panel and slips through the wall into the gap behind it

lines.text: Your press races down a wire to the controller. Which ignores it.
lines.see: An amber pulse runs along the wire up to the controller cabinet; it hits and dies, screen says IGNORED

lines.text: In America, a 1990 disability law makes lift doors wait.
lines.see: Controller screen switches to a hold timer, headline 1990 counts up

lines.text: At least three seconds, so someone in a wheelchair has time to get in.
lines.see: Inside the lift looking out: a wheelchair rolls in while 3 s counts down, then the doors close

lines.text: So lots of close buttons were quietly switched off. Except for firefighters.
lines.see: Back on the panel: the close button goes dead grey, then the fire service key switch lights amber

lines.text: And it's not just lifts. In 2004, New York had 3,250 crossing buttons.
lines.see: Camera rises up the shaft past every floor and out of the roof over a night city; thousands of crossing buttons light up, headline 3,250
A wave turns 2,500 of the lights grey, headline 2,500 counts up

lines.text: In the UK, though? Most close buttons actually work.
lines.see: Dive back down the shaft into the lift: press, and the doors close straight away

lines.text: So would you rather know, or keep pressing?
lines.see: Back to the same close button (loop to frame 0), question headline, comment bubble

facts.claim: The New York Times (27 Oct 2016) reported that the close-door function in US lifts faded into obsolescence a few years after the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990; Karen Penafiel of the National Elevator Industry said 'the riding public would not be able to make those doors close any faster'; firefighters and maintenance workers with keys can still use the buttons
Drexel University confirms the New York Times piece on placebo buttons (lifts and crossings) ran on 27 Oct 2016
ADA Standards for Accessible Design (1991), 4.10.8 Door Delay for Car Calls: 'The minimum time for elevator doors to remain fully open in response to a car call shall be 3 seconds'
Under the ADA, lift doors must stay open long enough for people using crutches, canes or wheelchairs to board
The New York Times (27 Feb 2004): 'more than 2,500 of the 3,250 walk buttons that still exist function essentially as mechanical placebos' in New York City
UK: 'close door' buttons are fully functional in most lifts (The Telegraph); a Lift and Escalator Industry Association spokesman said not all lifts have the button, but when present they work
Counterpoint: many US close buttons do work once the ADA minimum hold has passed, and the button is required in fire service mode, which is tested at annual inspections (ASME A17.1)
